claim: Kim, Kim, and Ryu adapt a haptic energy-bounding algorithm to sampled position-based impedance control (PBIC) of industrial robots. A recursive desired-force law estimates an instantaneous stiffness beta and clips it to two bounds: c1 represents the experimentally identified energy-dissipation capability of the impedance-controlled robot, while c2 is an online environment-stiffness estimate constrained not to exceed c1. Lemmas 1-3 and Theorem 1 show that the resulting feasible beta interval is sufficient for passivity of the modeled sampled robot-controller-environment network. DENSO robot contacts with 50, 100, and 180 kN/m cantilever locations show nominal behavior on softer contacts and stabilization of a stiff contact that destabilizes PBIC alone. However, in the stiff case the stable steady force is about 15 N rather than the desired 10 N and requires separate penetration-depth adjustment. The guarantee is conditional on passive environments, an accurate or conservative pose-dependent c1, effective linearized PBIC realization, measured energy, and the one-DOF network model; overestimating c1 can cause instability, so the paper's broad 'any uncertain environment' language should not be read as unconditional.
claim_locator: Section III-D-E, equations (18)-(29), Figures 5-6, Lemmas 1-3, Theorem 1
epistemic_status: qualified primary sampled-data passivity analysis and hardware demonstration: the energy inequalities provide a sufficient certificate for the idealized one-port PBIC network when c1/c2 bounds hold, while empirical support is a single six-axis robot tested only along one axis at three stiffness locations without repeated trials or statistical analysis
problem_and_setting: An industrial robot's impedance controller is normally designed for an assumed environment-stiffness range. Contact with a much stiffer surface can destabilize it, while designing for an extremely broad range makes response overdamped and sluggish. The paper seeks an outer sampled controller that preserves ordinary PBIC behavior within the nominal range but bounds energy and remains stable when actual passive environment stiffness is much larger than expected.
method_or_mechanism: The position-controlled industrial robot is first transformed to a target second-order impedance by an improved PBIC. A network representation separates continuous admittance, sample-and-hold, controller, and environment and writes a discrete passivity inequality. Target damping supplies dissipative energy that can offset energy generated by the sampled controller/environment interconnection. Desired force is updated recursively as Fd[n]=Fd[n-1]+beta[n] Delta xd[n], where unbounded beta equals a measured force/position increment and behaves like instantaneous stiffness. Lemma 1 caps beta by c1<=Bt/T; Lemmas 2-3 impose an interval derived from c2 and stored contact energy; Theorem 1 combines the bounds when c1>=c2. In practice c1 is identified offline by approaching sustained oscillation against a very stiff environment, while c2 is updated from a Hooke-law force/penetration stiffness estimate and clipped by c1.
content_summary: The paper distinguishes soft/nominal and unexpectedly stiff regimes. If environment stiffness Ke is below robot dissipation capacity c1, c2 can track Ke and adaptive EBA largely preserves PBIC force behavior. If Ke exceeds c1, beta/c2 bounding prevents instability but changes the steady force; the authors propose later reference-penetration adjustment ('prestability and postperformance') to recover the target. Experiments identify a DENSO position-loop model and implement a vertical one-DOF PBIC/adaptive EBA outer loop at approximately 50 Hz. A cantilever plate provides soft 50 kN/m, nominal 100 kN/m, and stiff 180 kN/m contacts; the controller is designed for 100 kN/m and 10 N, with c1=120 kN/m. At nominal stiffness PBIC and adaptive EBA behave similarly. In the soft case adaptive c2 removes the force error of constant-c2 haptic EBA. In the stiff case PBIC alone becomes unstable while adaptive EBA stabilizes contact, but steady force rises to about 15 N until penetration depth is iteratively reduced.
synthesis_role: Provides a sampled-data energy-certificate approach to environmental uncertainty that differs from force-error adaptive impedance: it protects interaction stability by bounding the realizable force-position slope using an empirically identified robot dissipation capacity, then adapts performance only inside that certified envelope.
development_link: The method extends the authors' haptic EBA from torque-controlled lightweight haptic devices to high-inertia position-controlled industrial robots and incorporates real-environment stored energy. It complements later energy tanks and passivity filters by bounding force updates directly rather than storing/releasing virtual energy or rate-limiting impedance matrices.

evidence.finding: PBIC renders a target impedance from an identified position-loop model, but its robust damping condition depends on the assumed environment-to-target stiffness ratio and can fail beyond that range.

The robot, sample-and-hold, controller, and environment are represented as a one-port network whose absorbed energy must exceed stored-energy growth; sample-and-hold phase cannot be omitted at the roughly 50 Hz outer loop.
A recursive force command uses measured incremental stiffness beta, which is clipped by c1 and c2-derived upper/lower bounds so dissipated robot energy covers sampled interaction energy.

evidence.locator: Section III-E, Lemmas 1-3 and Theorem 1, equations (18)-(29)
evidence.finding: If c1<=Bt/T, c1>=c2, and beta stays within the combined feasible interval, the two sufficient energy conditions hold simultaneously and the modeled interaction is passive.

Because unmodeled dynamics prevent setting c1 directly from Bt/T, c1 is identified experimentally against a very stiff contact; overestimating it can jeopardize stability and underestimating it degrades performance.
When Ke<=c1, c2 can match environment stiffness and preserve PBIC behavior; when Ke>c1, energy bounding stabilizes contact but distorts steady force, motivating reference-depth adjustment.

On a DENSO robot contacting 50, 100, and 180 kN/m points of a cantilever, adaptive EBA preserves nominal/soft behavior and stabilizes the 180 kN/m contact that is unstable under PBIC alone; the stiff steady force is approximately 15 N versus a 10 N target before trajectory adjustment.

The authors call for broader tests such as peg insertion and digging, delay-sensitive teleoperation, changing human/ground impedance, and more sophisticated estimation for complex environment structures.

boundary_conditions: The theorem applies to the paper's one-port sampled network with passive control input and environment; active environments or unmodeled energy sources are not covered by the broad uncertainty claim.
The main derivation and experiment are single-input single-output and one-DOF, with the position-controlled robot assumed effectively canceled into a target linear mass-damper-stiffness admittance.
The certificate depends on c1 not exceeding actual pose-dependent dissipation capacity; the paper explicitly warns that overestimated c1 can cause instability.
c1 is found empirically using near-oscillatory contact against a very stiff environment and may vary over the task-space pose, tooling, payload, wear, and low-level controller.

The simple Hooke-law c2 estimate presumes identifiable contact location and elastic stiffness; complex, hysteretic, viscoelastic, frictional, moving, or discontinuous environments may degrade force performance.
Passivity guarantees stability only for the modeled interconnection and does not bound peak impact force, injury, workpiece damage, actuator saturation, or commanded trajectory safety.
For stiffness above c1 the target force is not automatically maintained; a separate iterative penetration-depth heuristic is required after stability is obtained.
Hardware evidence covers one robot, one axis, one cantilever, three stiffness points, approximately 50 Hz outer control, and descriptive traces without repetitions or inferential statistics.
assumptions: The identified minimum-phase position-loop model and PBIC realize the target impedance closely enough for the network energy decomposition.
The target damping provides at least the dissipation represented by the conservative c1 bound across the relevant workspace and operating state.
Force and penetration increments are measured accurately enough to compute beta, contact energy, and stiffness estimate.
The environment is passive and its stored-energy contribution is captured by the controller-environment energy term.
c2 is always kept positive and no greater than c1, regardless of estimator delay or error.
The outer-loop sample-and-hold timing matches the energy accounting and the low-level position controller remains stable under generated commands.

reported: PBIC designed for 100 kN/m becomes unstable when tested at the 180 kN/m stiff contact.
Constant-c2 haptic EBA produces substantial force error on the softer 50 kN/m contact.
Adaptive EBA stabilizes the stiff contact but produces about 15 N rather than the desired 10 N because c2 is capped by c1.
Overestimating c1 can jeopardize stability; underestimating it preserves stability but degrades performance.
Broader complex-task, teleoperation, human/ground contact, and environment-estimator validation remains future work.
inferred: Changes in payload, pose, friction, low-level gains, temperature, or wear after offline calibration can make the stored c1 unsafe or unnecessarily conservative.
Near-oscillation calibration against a very stiff surface is itself an operationally risky and subjective identification procedure unless instrumented safeguards are added.
Noise or near-zero displacement increments can make instantaneous stiffness beta ill-conditioned and trigger aggressive clipping or force-command discontinuities.
The postperformance penetration adjustment can be slow and may violate transient force limits even though the interaction remains passive.
